transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-29
Start: 10:00 AM UTC
Duration: 45m
Attendees: Maya Patel, Jared Kim - Redwood; Sam Ortega, Priya Rao, Liam Chen - Eddybridge

[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick agenda — run through the latest bench numbers, call out any anomalies, discuss config tweaks, and confirm next steps. Sam, you good to kick off?
[00:12] Sam Ortega: Yeah, thanks Maya. We ran the week-2 set of tests. Wanted to call out two things up front: p50 improved a lot with the quantize change and routing, but we still see p95 spikes during long-contexts.
[00:28] Jared Kim: Right, so the numbers I have — p50 for Redwood test harness is around 120ms end-to-end for the 256 token microbench, baseline (IncumbentAI) is ~210ms. p95 is 320ms vs baseline 540ms. Throughput at concurrency 8 was roughly 380 reqs/min for Redwood vs 360 reqs/min baseline.
[00:46] Priya Rao: Those are good head-to-head numbers, but our production pattern has a heavy tail — a lot of 1k token inference and KV-cache misses which is where we saw the p95 spikes.
[01:03] Liam Chen: Also want to mention we observed an occasional CPU-starve on the proxy host when batching hit a weird boundary. Might be our test harness.
[01:15] Jared Kim: Makes sense. We pushed a couple of runtime knobs this morning — smaller batch windows for longer sequences and warmed the KV cash, sorry KV cache, on the longer dialogs. That dropped p95 by about 80ms in our lab run.
[01:30] Sam Ortega: Cool, can you clarify "smaller batch windows"? Are we increasing frequency of micro-batches?
[01:36] Jared Kim: Yeah, so instead of waiting 50ms to accumulate tokens we used a 20ms timer for sequences flagged as long-running so long sequences won't queue behind many short calls. It's a hybrid batching policy — short ones still batch aggressively to save cost.
[01:51] Maya Patel: One thing the sales ops team asked us to be explicit about — the cost delta if you switch to a dedicated pool. Jared, can you give ballpark?
[02:01] Jared Kim: Ballpark wise, for your workload profile — with 8 dedicated slots on A100-style capacity, your per-million-token unit cost comes down roughly 25-35% vs hosted. That excludes egress/data transfer or infra discounts. We'll put numbers in the workbook.
[02:18] Priya Rao: We're also evaluating CloudEndpoint for dedicated. Their public docs show similar latencies but pricing is different. Any known tradeoffs?
[02:29] Maya Patel: From our side, tradeoffs are predictable throughput and the tooling for routing and KV caching. Redwood Optimize suggestions about quant profiles gave most of the wins here. Also our rollout/playbook can do canary by percent and auto-fallback to a cheaper model variant.
[02:46] Sam Ortega: About the fallbacks — what happens to quality when you fallback to a quantized model? We can't degrade clinical-grade outputs beyond certain tolerances.
[02:55] Jared Kim: Great question. We run model evals tied to your prompt sets — we saw a BLEU-ish style delta under 1.2% for the 8-bit quant profile we used. I'll push the eval artifacts. But yes, if you want, we can pin the critical routes to non-quantized model variants and only use quantize for less-sensitive calls.
[03:15] Priya Rao: That would be ideal. We'll mark two routes as sensitive — claims ingestion and triage response.
[03:22] Maya Patel: Noted. Sam, you had said there were KV-cache misses causing spikes — is that mostly warm-up on new sessions or random contextual changes?
[03:32] Sam Ortega: Mostly warm-up. Our traffic has new user sessions frequently so prefix cache hit rate is around 62% in your lab runs. If we can bump that to 80% would reduce tail a lot.
[03:43] Jared Kim: For prefix cache hit improvement we recommend: (a) increase prefix size to 3 tokens for your standard prompts, (b) pin frequently used agent prompts into the cache on startup, and (c) sticky routing for session affinity — small overhead but big cache retention.
[03:58] Liam Chen: Sticky routing means more state on the load balancer. Our ops team is cautious about that. Any lighter options?
[04:06] Jared Kim: You can use probabilistic affinity or use request-signature-based KV keys — that's what we suggested in the doc. It keeps the LB stateless. We'll include config snippet.
[04:17] Sam Ortega: On the throughput front, we saw a throughput plateau after concurrency 12. Any suggestions?
[04:24] Jared Kim: Plateaus usually due to memory bandwidth on the GPU or the tokenization CPU step. Two levers — increase slot count (more parallel model replicas) or optimize tokenization on the client side (batch tokenization before sending). For immediate wins, adding 2 more slots in the dedicated spike should move the needle.
[04:40] Maya Patel: Let's propose a 2-week dedicated spike: 10 slots, moderate autoscale thresholds, start with 10% traffic split as canary. Jared to propose slot sizing.
[04:50] Sam Ortega: That sounds good. We'll need security sign-off first — SOC2 and KMS integration questions.
[04:57] Maya Patel: On SOC2, Redwood has a live report and an ISO summary — I'll attach. For KMS we support customer-managed keys and HSM — Jared, remind them about key rotation controls.
[05:07] Jared Kim: Yep. We can integrate with your AWS KMS or other provider. Keys never leave the HSM, audit logs are shipped to your SIEM via our secure webhook. We'll include the technical runbook.
[05:19] Priya Rao: Do you support VPC-only private deployment or do we have to use a hybrid? We need data to stay in our VPC for some flows.
[05:27] Maya Patel: Yes, Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem packaging. For the spike we can do dedicated capacity inside our hosted VPC peering with your account or we can provision an isolated VPC if needed. We can loop in the infra engineer to sort routing.
[05:41] Sam Ortega: Ok great. A few anomalies from the lab logs — there's an occasional 504 from the model runtime at 3:14am UTC in your test run. We flagged it in the perf workbook. Any idea?
[05:51] Jared Kim: We saw that too; I think it collated with a maintenance window on the underlying infra and our autoscaler got briefly overwhelmed by a burst. We added a guard to extend busy windows during spikes to avoid tearing down warmed replicas. That fix is in staging.
[06:06] Liam Chen: Can you share the incident trace? Our SREs want the headers and the stack.
[06:11] Jared Kim: I'll export the traces and share the link.
[06:15] Maya Patel: Quick check — success criteria for this pilot. Sam, what's the threshold that would make you move to Dedicated?
[06:22] Sam Ortega: Two things: 1) a 30% or greater reduction in median latency vs current vendor during our peak workload, and 2) predictable p95 under 500ms for 95% of traffic. If those hold for two weeks in the dedicated spike we'll consider expanding.
[06:36] Maya Patel: Great. We'll codify that in the workbook.
[06:39] Priya Rao: One last ops ask — can you provide a sample autoscale policy and the cost delta at the 90th percentile usage?
[06:47] Jared Kim: Yep, will include autoscale example — target CPU/GPU util thresholds and burst policies. Cost delta at 90th pct in initial calc was about 28% lower than hosted baseline when amortized across the slot commit. We'll show both amortized and peak cost.
[07:04] Sam Ortega: Perfect. Anything else?
[07:07] Maya Patel: Quick recap of next steps, then we'll close.
[07:10] Priya Rao: also small nit — in the perf worksheets some model names got mangled ("Redwood Dedicate" instead of "Redwood Dedicated"). Minor but I'll send a note.
[07:19] Jared Kim: Thanks, we'll clean up naming.
[07:21] Maya Patel: Recap: Jared to propose dedicated slot sizing and canary plan; Maya to send perf workbook, SOC2 and ISO docs; Customer to share traffic CSV and security stakeholders. We'll schedule kick-off for the dedicated spike once workbook and questionnaire are in.
[07:35] Sam Ortega: Sounds good. Appreciate the fast turnaround.
[07:38] Maya Patel: Thanks all, we'll follow up in email with links.

End of meeting. Links shared: perf_workbook_v2.xlsx; soc2_redwood_redacted.pdf; trace_export_20260328.zip

Notes on transcription: some words mis-transcribed (KV cash -> KV cache); occasional overlaps; speaker labels accurate for most parts but may show AE/SE swapped for short interjections.
